title: Chapter 8: The Treat Crossing
blurb: A nine-year-old asks what time the treat crossing leaves, and a scarfed stranger has promised her a door at ten.

blocks.text: On day fifty-eight, at twenty to eight in the morning, a girl in a red knitted hood stood on her toes at the Exchange Desk and asked what time the treat crossing left.
Miss Tolliver looked at me. I was at the desk because I had been measuring the dawn packet's seal, which is not my job any more. It was true to the degree.
"The man in the Survey coat said ten," said the girl. "He just didn't say which door."
There is no treat crossing. There has never been a treat crossing.
Footnote: I checked the Standing Orders that morning, twice, in case I had been wrong about that for three years.

Her name was Nell Pardoe. She was nine, "and a half, nearly." Her mother scrubbed the Hall's front steps on Mondays and Thursdays, which was why Nell knew where the Hall was, and why the porter had let her wait inside where it was warm.
I took the clerk's spare stool so I wasn't taller than her.
"Which man?"

"The kind one. With the scarf." She showed me with both hands, up over her nose. "He sat on the bench by the bridge on Saturday and said was I Nell Pardoe who didn't want to go to the coast. And I said yes. I mean, I said I was. And he said there's a girl who said yes. She lives by the sea at Gannet Head and she's just like me, and would I like to meet her, as a treat. He said I'd be back for tea."
"What coast?"

She explained, the way children explain things to adults who should know already. Two summers ago her father, Will Pardoe, a lighterman, was offered a pilot's place at Gannet Head. He asked Nell whether she'd like to live by the sea. She said no.
"Because of Biscuit," she said. "Biscuit's our cat. Cats don't like moving. Everyone knows that."
So he turned it down, and the Pardoes stayed in Tessary, and that was the end of it. In the Bole.
Footnote: most decisions aren't hinges. A family's whole life turning on a seven-year-old and a cat could be one. I wrote it down anyway. I write everything down.
"What's your name?" said Nell.
"Ardent."
"That's a surname."
"It's the one I use."
Footnote: the other one is borrowed. I'd rather give a child the one I'm sure of.
Cressida came down at eight for the packets. I met her at the foot of the stairs, which she dislikes.
"Cartographer. I'd like a case."
"What case?"
"A man in a Survey coat has promised a nine-year-old a crossing at ten this morning."
"And the evidence he exists?"
"A nine-year-old, a bench and a scarf." I gave her the rest. "He knew her decision. He knew what she said at seven, and which way. Porters don't know what a hinge is. He does."
"You think she's a hinge-maker."
"I think he thinks so."

Cressida looked across the threshold room at the red hood on the stool. Then she walked to the nearest of the nine doors, the iron-studded one in the south wall, and stood in it, and read in her ordinary voice, as if she were reading a requisition:
"Pardoe's coast, yes."
A sounding spends nothing. It opens nothing. If the branch exists, the door warms, and that's all.
The door warmed. I held the back of my hand near the frame, and it was like standing by a bread oven.
Cressida took a census card from her coat and wrote on it in pinned ink. Hinges: one. Pardoe's coast, two summers ago. Mirrors: everything on the other side of it.

"She's a hinge-maker," she said. "It happens. Plenty of people make one. Some make one before they can spell it." She capped her pen. "There's a custom: never cross into your mirror. It's a superstition, Ardent. Nobody has ever shown me a bill for it. But nobody takes a child through my doors as a treat, whoever's custom it is. You have your case."
At the window end of the Exchange Desk, Verity Sallis put her pencil down.
She went the colour of the desk blotter, which is white.
Brisk arrived at a quarter past eight with her kit bag and took one look at Nell.
"Toast," she said. "Kitchen. You and me."
"How old are you?" said Nell.
"Forty-four."
"You're not."
"Thank you, pet. I've been practising."
They went. I watched Verity. She folded her tables into their card and walked out of the threshold room, not fast, into the cold yard where the carters turn.
I followed her, and I took my time doing it.

On day sixteen, at the Ferrytown customs house, her counterpart had called through a closing door: ask her what happened in Kittering Lane when she was nine. I had carried that for forty-two days. I hadn't asked. It had never been the right moment, and I didn't want to be the person who asked it at the wrong one.
She stood by the pump with her arms folded.

"Sallis," I said. "Day sixteen, your counterpart told me to ask you about Kittering Lane. I didn't. I'm asking now, because there's a child in the kitchen and less than two hours, and you went white when the Cartographer said superstition. You don't have to answer. If you do, I'll treat it as evidence, not gossip."
"Seventy-four percent you'd ask me today," said Verity. "I worked it out at the desk. I was hoping for the other twenty-six."
"Sorry."

"Don't be. It's tidier." She looked at the pump handle, not at me. "I was nine. My grandmother lived across the estuary, on Kittering Lane. My mother put me on the ferry stage to go and stay the winter with her. I didn't get on. I was frightened of the water. I screamed until she took me home. That's all. In the Bole, that's all it was."
"And somewhere else you got on."

"Three weeks later my aunt sounded it at the Ninefold, for fun. She was a cartographer. 'Sallis's ferry, boarded.' The door warmed. She was delighted. She said I'd made a hinge before I could do long division, and that deserved a treat."
There it was. The same word. I didn't say anything. I'd have written it down if I'd had a pen in my hand.

"She took me across. The Survey called the branch Kittering Lane, after my grandmother's street. In Kittering Lane I'd got on the ferry, and stayed the winter, and then stayed for good. My parents sold up and moved across to be near me. A family on the wrong side of a river. That's all a hinge is, sometimes." She swallowed. "I met her. Me. She had my cardigan, and she could row."
"How long did you stay?"

"One afternoon. My aunt stood in the open doorway first for a long time, showing me the street, and nothing happened, because standing in the doorway isn't entering. Then we went in. At dusk she read us home. She stepped through first and I stepped through second, and the door went cold behind me. Not shut. Cold. The whole branch in one breath."
"Like Brackwater."

"I read your Greyfell report. Yes. Like Brackwater." She unfolded her arms and folded them the other way. "The Survey filed it as natural decay. 'Pin died during a family visit.' My aunt wrote that line herself. She gave up her licence that winter and never crossed again."
"And afterwards?"

"Afterwards, for a year, I lived her life." She said it the way she reads a table. "Not mine. Hers. I'd wake up knowing how to row. I knew the hymn they sang at the chapel on Kittering Lane, and I've never been inside it. I knew a girl called Bettany who was my best friend, and I've never met her. Some weeks a fact a night, then nothing for a month, then three at once. All of it landed on me, because I was the nearest me. That's what I meant, Ardent. Windfall doesn't only bring back what's yours. It brings you everything she was. And then it stopped, because there was nothing left of her to fall."
I didn't make a joke. I can, but I didn't.

"Here's the rule your Cartographer calls a superstition," said Verity. "Your hinge splits the Fan into your side and the other side. If you leave any branch on the other side, or you stay seven midnights and owe rent there, the swap reaches for the fact that branch agrees with least. For a hinge-maker on her own other side, that's the hinge. It's top of the order. Ballast never beats it. And a hinge can't be traded, so the hinge closes instead. Everything on the other side of it falls, and you're thrown home as it goes."
"And the doorway?"

"The doorway is safe. You can stand in it all day. It's stepping through that dooms it. Your exit, or your first rent." She looked at me at last. "That isn't custom. It's a mechanism. I was the experiment."
I was frightened, so I made a list.

1. Nell Pardoe is a hinge-maker, and the man knows her hinge. 2. He called it a treat. 3. If she steps into anything on her other side and comes back out, and he has promised she'll be back for tea, the girl who said yes falls, and Gannet Head with her, and everything split from that side in the last two years. 4. Nell will be thrown home. She will be nine and unhurt. For a year she'll wake up knowing how to live by the sea.
Footnote: I made that list in my head, by the pump. I'm putting it on the bill now, because a bill should be complete.
"I'm on the case," said Verity.
"I didn't ask you."
"Eighty-one percent you were about to." She was already walking back. "And you'll want a door. You've got nine."
She spread her tables on the Exchange Desk, and Cressida and I stood on either side of them like people at a deathbed.

"Geometry first," said Verity. "Every route into her other side starts with her hinge. 'Pardoe's coast, yes.' Then whatever he likes after it. So he needs a door that reaches a branch younger than two years. Every Ninefold door is old enough. All nine are medieval. What matters is which one is least likely to have been altered over there, because altering a door on either side kills it."
"And your tables know that?"

"My tables know every alteration any near-branch desk has ever reported to us, and how fast Tessary rebuilds things." Her pencil went down a column. "North door: re-hung in two near branches. West door: renovated in Saltings. South door: eighteen percent. The Chapter door: seventy-one."

The Chapter door is the oldest of the nine: low, in the north-east corner, no handle, a step worn hollow in the middle. In every Tessary the Survey has a record of, it's listed, and nobody is allowed to touch it.
"Seventy-one," said Cressida.
"And the other twenty-nine are mostly the south door."
Cressida looked at Verity for a long moment.

"Cartographer," said Verity. "You said nobody had ever shown you a bill for it. I was nine. I didn't have a bill. I had a year of somebody else's life. I'll write it out for you in pinned ink if you want it."
"Later," said Cressida. "Where do you want me?"
That was Cressida saying she'd been wrong. She doesn't use the word. She uses the next question.

Mrs Pardoe came in from the steps at half past nine, red to the elbows. Cressida told her the plain parts and none of the frightening ones. Mrs Pardoe said Nell was going home this minute. Cressida said the man knew where Nell sat on Saturdays, and the safest place in Tessary for the next half hour was the room with the four of us in it. Mrs Pardoe stayed, with one hand on her daughter's shoulder.
The plan:
1. Nell and her mother at the Exchange Desk, with Cressida. 2. Brisk at the south door. 3. Verity and me by the Chapter door. 4. The porter on the gate, looking for a scarf.
Footnote: it was a good plan. It had a hole in it the shape of a nine-year-old.
Ten o'clock is when the far crews come home.

The Hall clock began to strike, and the north door and the west door opened within a breath of each other. Two crews came through, eleven surveyors with kit bags, and the threshold room filled with Survey coats, wet boots and people calling for tea. I had stood in that room at ten o'clock a hundred times. I had never once thought of it as cover.

A man in a grey Survey coat stepped out of the crowd beside the Chapter door. Hat to the brows. Scarf to the eyes. No rank tabs, and a cut of coat I didn't know. He didn't look at me. He stood in the door and read, too low to hear, and the Chapter door opened.
Across the room, Brisk began to count.
"One."

Nell saw him. A nine-year-old can get out of any grip; I've since read the literature. She was off the stool and across the floor between two kit bags before her mother had closed her hand on nothing.
"Two."
He held out his hand. She took it. They stepped up onto the hollow step, into the open doorway.
"Three."
Through the door was a threshold room very like ours, lamps unlit, nobody in it.
"Four."

I was there. Verity was faster. Verity Sallis, who has never touched a doorframe in her life, put her left hand flat on the Chapter door's frame and closed her right fist in the back of Nell's red hood.
"Five."
I took Nell's wrist. She was in the doorway, not through it. Standing in the open doorway is not entering.
The man was half a step ahead of her, on the far edge of the sill. He looked down at Nell's hand in his. He looked at Verity's hand on the stone. His other hand went into his coat and came out empty.
"Six."
He let go of her. Gently, one finger at a time, the way you put down something you don't want to break.
"Seven."
He stepped through.
I could have caught his sleeve. I had her wrist instead. I would do the same sums again.
"Eight."
He walked away into the unlit room without looking back, and the far side of the door was a dark shape getting smaller.
"He said I'd be back for tea," said Nell.
"Nine."
The Chapter door shut.
Mrs Pardoe got there a breath later and didn't say anything at all. She just held on.
"Was that the treat?" said Nell, into her mother's coat.
Cressida knelt. A Cartographer of sixty, on a threshold-room floor, in front of two crews and a clerk.
"No," she said. "Go home with your mother. Feed your cat."
They went home.
Miss Tolliver had already logged it. That's her job, and she does it in any weather: Ten o'clock. Chapter door. Opened from the Bole side. Reader unknown, route not heard. One out.
I went back through the log to the start of the quarter. Nobody had ever logged him arriving.
Footnote: his reading spent the Bole's opening to wherever he'd gone, for the rest of the day. Nobody could have followed him before dawn. Nobody knew where to.
Nobody saw his face. I've been asked since. Hat, scarf, a pair of eyes, and I couldn't tell you their colour. I'd like that on the record, because I'm not proud of it.
Verity stood by the Chapter door with her left hand held a little away from her side, as if the stone were still on it.
"Sallis," said Cressida.
"Cartographer."
"Pinned ink. Tonight. Everything you remember of Kittering Lane."
"Yes, Cartographer."
Cressida took out Nell's census card and wrote one more line under Mirrors, in pinned ink, and showed it to nobody. I read it anyway, the right way up: Do not admit.
Swap bill for day fifty-eight: no crew crossing. Nothing of ours spent. One opening spent from the Bole side, by a man who isn't in our log.

Footnote: twenty-two days to my Chainman's Walk. Verity designed its hazards and won't tell me what they are. I had decided to be civil to her anyway. I found that morning that I didn't need to decide.

On day fifty-nine I went to the kit room at seven for a measuring chain. I wanted the Chapter door's dimensions on file and its mason's mark drawn, because yesterday it had been used against us and I didn't know its size.
Gideon was humming his tune, the one nobody in the Bole knows. He found me the chain, and the good chalk, and asked whether I'd eaten.
"You want a dog, chuck," he said. "Lad who measures doors before breakfast wants a dog. I had a lurcher when I was a boy. Best dog in Tessary. She was called—"
He stopped, with the chalk in his hand.

"Called," he said. "Pip." He frowned at the chalk. "No. That's not right. That's somebody else's dog, that is." Then he laughed, the big kit-room laugh. "Seventy-four and a half, sir. Things go walkabout."
He went back to humming. He laughed it off, so I did too.

The threshold room at seven is empty except for Miss Tolliver and the dawn packets. I knelt at the Chapter door with the chain. Thirty-four inches by seventy-one. A mason's mark low on the left jamb, like a bird's foot.
Under the bench beside the door, against the skirting, where a boot would kick it in a crowd, there was a card.
Plain card, cut to the Hall's size, ordinary ink. I knew the layout before I'd read a word of it.

Branch: Gannet Light. Distance: ten. Route, in Bole notation, in our order: Pardoe's coast, yes. Then nine hinges more, every one of them younger than hers. Hinge-maker: Kettlewell, J., schoolmistress. Filed: Far Map, day thirty-eight.
A pin card. A far branch, on the other side of a nine-year-old's hinge.
I walked to the Far Map drawers with it in my hand. The original was where it belonged, on Hall board with the Survey's stamp, filed three weeks ago. Same route. Same words. Same order.
Somebody had copied one of our cards, and the first name on its route was hers.
